claim: Leptospirosis is an emerging infectious disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira spp.
source: Leptospirosis is an emerging infectious disease caused by pathogenic Leptospira spp.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about leptospirosis.

claim: Humans and some mammals can develop severe forms of leptospirosis accompanied by a dysregulated inflammatory response, which often results in death.
source: Humans and some mammals can develop severe forms of leptospirosis accompanied by a dysregulated inflammatory response, which often results in death.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about severe leptospirosis outcomes.

claim: Leptospires were able to multiply in the intestine of hamsters.
source: Our study showed that leptospires were able to multiply in the intestine, cause pathological injury, and induce intestinal and systemic inflammatory responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing leptospiral proliferation in the ileum and colon as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Leptospires cause pathological injury in the intestine.
source: Our study showed that leptospires were able to multiply in the intestine, cause pathological injury, and induce intestinal and systemic inflammatory responses.
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating intestinal structure disruption.

claim: Leptospires induce intestinal and systemic inflammatory responses.
source: Our study showed that leptospires were able to multiply in the intestine, cause pathological injury, and induce intestinal and systemic inflammatory responses.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data showing upregulation of inflammatory markers in Figure 1D-I.

claim: Leptospira infection changed the composition of the gut microbiota of hamsters with an expansion of Proteobacteria.
source: 16S rRNA gene sequencing analysis revealed that Leptospira infection changed the composition of the gut microbiota of hamsters with an expansion of Proteobacteria.
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: Gut barrier permeability was increased after Leptospira infection.
source: In addition, gut barrier permeability was increased after infection, as reflected by a decrease in the expression of tight junctions.
evidence: Supported by FITC-dextran permeability assay data shown in Figure 3A and tight junction gene expression data in Figure 3B-F.

claim: Leptospira infection decreased the expression of tight junctions.
source: In addition, gut barrier permeability was increased after infection, as reflected by a decrease in the expression of tight junctions.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data showing decreased ZO-1, Claudin-3, JAMA, and Mucin-2 in Figure 3B-F.

claim: Translocated Proteobacteria were found in the intestinal epithelium of moribund hamsters.
source: Translocated Proteobacteria were found in the intestinal epithelium of moribund hamsters, as determined by fluorescence in situ hybridization, with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in the serum.
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Moribund hamsters had elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in the serum.
source: Translocated Proteobacteria were found in the intestinal epithelium of moribund hamsters, as determined by fluorescence in situ hybridization, with elevated lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels in the serum.
evidence: Supported by LPS measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gut microbiota depletion reduced the survival time after Leptospira infection.
source: Moreover, gut microbiota depletion reduced the survival time, increased the leptospiral load, and promoted the expression of proinflammatory cytokines after Leptospira infection.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Gut microbiota depletion increased the leptospiral load after Leptospira infection.
source: Moreover, gut microbiota depletion reduced the survival time, increased the leptospiral load, and promoted the expression of proinflammatory cytokines after Leptospira infection.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing increased leptospiral load in Figure 5J.

claim: Gut microbiota depletion promoted the expression of proinflammatory cytokines after Leptospira infection.
source: Moreover, gut microbiota depletion reduced the survival time, increased the leptospiral load, and promoted the expression of proinflammatory cytokines after Leptospira infection.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: Fecal filtration from moribund hamsters increased the transcription of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4 in macrophages compared with those from uninfected hamsters.
source: Intriguingly, fecal filtration and serum from moribund hamsters both increased the transcription of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4 in macrophages compared with those from uninfected hamsters.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: Serum from moribund hamsters increased the transcription of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4 in macrophages compared with those from uninfected hamsters.
source: Intriguingly, fecal filtration and serum from moribund hamsters both increased the transcription of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4 in macrophages compared with those from uninfected hamsters.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F-I.

claim: The stimulating activities of fecal filtration and serum from moribund hamsters were inhibited by LPS neutralization using polymyxin B.
source: These stimulating activities were inhibited by LPS neutralization using polymyxin B.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced cytokine expression after PMB treatment in Figure 6J-Q.

claim: LPS neutralization therapy significantly improved the survival rates in severe leptospirosis when used in combination with antibiotic therapy.
source: Based on our findings, we identified an LPS neutralization therapy that significantly improved the survival rates in severe leptospirosis when used in combination with antibiotic therapy or polyclonal antibody therapy.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: LPS neutralization therapy significantly improved the survival rates in severe leptospirosis when used in combination with polyclonal antibody therapy.
source: Based on our findings, we identified an LPS neutralization therapy that significantly improved the survival rates in severe leptospirosis when used in combination with antibiotic therapy or polyclonal antibody therapy.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Leptospira interrogans impacts approximately 1 million people, resulting in 60,000 deaths every year.
source: Leptospira interrogans impacts approximately 1 million people, resulting in 60,000 deaths every year (Coburn et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coburn et al., 2021.

claim: In human leptospirosis, the clinical manifestations can range from mild illness to multiorgan failure, characterized by jaundice, kidney, and liver failure, and even death.
source: In human leptospirosis, the clinical manifestations can range from mild illness to multiorgan failure, characterized by jaundice, kidney, and liver failure, and even death (Haake and Levett, 2015; Maia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haake and Levett, 2015 and Maia et al., 2022.

claim: Leptospirosis is often misdiagnosed as other febrile diseases.
source: Currently, one important challenge is that leptospirosis is often misdiagnosed as other febrile diseases, and once the optimal treatment period is missed, leptospirosis quickly develops into the severe form, which often ends in death (Coutinho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coutinho et al., 2014.

claim: Once the optimal treatment period is missed, leptospirosis quickly develops into the severe form, which often ends in death.
source: Currently, one important challenge is that leptospirosis is often misdiagnosed as other febrile diseases, and once the optimal treatment period is missed, leptospirosis quickly develops into the severe form, which often ends in death (Coutinho et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coutinho et al., 2014.

claim: Antibiotic treatment is often useless in severe leptospirosis and even aggravates it, called the Jarisch–Herxheimer Reaction.
source: However, antibiotic treatment is often useless in severe leptospirosis and even aggravates it, called the Jarisch–Herxheimer Reaction (Guerrier and D'Ortenzio, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Guerrier and D'Ortenzio, 2013.

claim: Ninety percent of infected humans may resolve spontaneously while 10% of patients are designated as susceptible hosts.
source: Ninety percent of infected humans may resolve spontaneously while 10% of patients are designated as susceptible hosts (Cagliero et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cagliero et al., 2018.

claim: Intestinal bleeding is a common but neglected symptom of severe leptospirosis in humans and hamster.
source: Intestinal bleeding is a common but neglected symptom of severe leptospirosis in humans and hamster (Alventosa Mateu, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alventosa Mateu, 2017.

claim: The intestine harbors a densely populated resident microbial community, which consists of bacteria, viruses, and fungi, called microbiota.
source: The intestine harbors a densely populated resident microbial community, which consists of bacteria, viruses, and fungi, called microbiota (Kamada et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kamada et al., 2013.

claim: Gut dysbiosis has been linked to increased susceptibility to disseminated bacterial infections and sepsis in humans.
source: Gut dysbiosis has been linked to increased susceptibility to disseminated bacterial infections and sepsis in humans.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge in the field of microbiome research.

claim: Studies of patients in intensive care units (ICUs) have found that dysbiosis increases the risk of nosocomial infections, sepsis, and mortality.
source: In addition, studies of patients in intensive care units (ICUs) have found that dysbiosis increases the risk of nosocomial infections, sepsis, and mortality (McDonald et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDonald et al., 2020.

claim: The gut microbiota contributed to the defense against Leptospira infection in mice, a resistant model of leptospirosis, without obvious intestinal lesions or increased intestinal permeability.
source: Our previous study proved that the gut microbiota contributed to the defense against Leptospira infection in mice, a resistant model of leptospirosis, without obvious intestinal lesions or increased intestinal permeability (Xie et al., 2022), while diarrhea was a common symptom in the late leptospirosis of hamster.
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2022.

claim: Diarrhea was a common symptom in the late leptospirosis of hamster.
source: Our previous study proved that the gut microbiota contributed to the defense against Leptospira infection in mice, a resistant model of leptospirosis, without obvious intestinal lesions or increased intestinal permeability (Xie et al., 2022), while diarrhea was a common symptom in the late leptospirosis of hamster.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The gut microbiota is closely related to the homeostasis of the intestine.
source: As is known, the gut microbiota is closely related to the homeostasis of the intestine (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2022.

claim: The variation of the gut microbiota mediated the different susceptibility to cholera infection.
source: A previous study demonstrated that the variation of the gut microbiota mediated the different susceptibility to cholera infection (Alavi et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alavi et al., 2020.

claim: Subcutaneous infection with leptospires led to intestinal dissemination.
source: Recently, Inamasu et al. reported that subcutaneous infection with leptospires led to intestinal dissemination (Inamasu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inamasu et al., 2022.

claim: Subcutaneous challenge and intraperitoneal challenge both led to leptospiral proliferation in the ileum and colon.
source: Our study indicated that subcutaneous challenge and intraperitoneal challenge both led to leptospiral proliferation in the ileum and colon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1B.

claim: There were approximately seven times more leptospires in the colon than in the ileums at articulo mortis (AM) post infection after intraperitoneal challenge.
source: There were approximately seven times more leptospires in the colon than in the ileums at articulo mortis (AM) post infection (p.i.) after intraperitoneal challenge (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hamsters infected by intraperitoneal challenge had shortened survival time compared with hamsters infected by subcutaneous challenge.
source: Hamsters infected by intraperitoneal challenge had shortened survival time compared with hamsters infected by subcutaneous challenge (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: L. interrogans infection disrupted the intestinal structure, caused bleeding, and led to the infiltration of inflammatory cells.
source: L. interrogans infection disrupted the intestinal structure, caused bleeding, and led to the infiltration of inflammatory cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: L. interrogans infection promoted the inflammatory response in the colons as determined by the upregulated gene expression of lipocalin 2 (Lcn2)/neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL).
source: In addition, L. interrogans infection promoted the inflammatory response in the colons as determined by the upregulated gene expression of lipocalin 2 (Lcn2)/neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), a marker of intestinal inflammation (Kitamoto et al., 2020), TNF-α, IL-1β, Nos2, and TLR4 (a well-known receptor of LPS that is vital against Leptospira infection [Viriyakosol et al., 2006] and the downregulated gene expression of IL-10) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D-I and citations to Kitamoto et al., 2020 and Viriyakosol et al., 2006.

claim: Lcn2/NGAL is a marker of intestinal inflammation.
source: In addition, L. interrogans infection promoted the inflammatory response in the colons as determined by the upregulated gene expression of lipocalin 2 (Lcn2)/neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), a marker of intestinal inflammation (Kitamoto et al., 2020), TNF-α, IL-1β, Nos2, and TLR4 (a well-known receptor of LPS that is vital against Leptospira infection [Viriyakosol et al., 2006] and the downregulated gene expression of IL-10) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kitamoto et al., 2020.

claim: TLR4 is a well-known receptor of LPS that is vital against Leptospira infection.
source: In addition, L. interrogans infection promoted the inflammatory response in the colons as determined by the upregulated gene expression of lipocalin 2 (Lcn2)/neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), a marker of intestinal inflammation (Kitamoto et al., 2020), TNF-α, IL-1β, Nos2, and TLR4 (a well-known receptor of LPS that is vital against Leptospira infection [Viriyakosol et al., 2006] and the downregulated gene expression of IL-10) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by citation to Viriyakosol et al., 2006.

claim: L. interrogans infection downregulated the gene expression of IL-10 in the colons.
source: In addition, L. interrogans infection promoted the inflammatory response in the colons as determined by the upregulated gene expression of lipocalin 2 (Lcn2)/neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), a marker of intestinal inflammation (Kitamoto et al., 2020), TNF-α, IL-1β, Nos2, and TLR4 (a well-known receptor of LPS that is vital against Leptospira infection [Viriyakosol et al., 2006] and the downregulated gene expression of IL-10) (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The gene expression of TLR2 and TLR9 was significantly increased in the AM group compared with the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the gene expression of TLR2 and TLR9 was significantly increased, while TLR3, TLR5, and TLR7 showed no obvious difference in the AM group compared with the D0 group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and E.

claim: TLR3, TLR5, and TLR7 showed no obvious difference in the AM group compared with the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the gene expression of TLR2 and TLR9 was significantly increased, while TLR3, TLR5, and TLR7 showed no obvious difference in the AM group compared with the D0 group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Leptospira infection can cause leptospiremia and cytokine storms at late stages.
source: It is well known that Leptospira infection can cause leptospiremia and cytokine storms at late stages (Cagliero et al., 2018; Limothai et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cagliero et al., 2018 and Limothai et al., 2021.

claim: The gene expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-10 was increased in the blood of the AM group compared with that of the D0 group.
source: Our results also proved that the gene expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-10 was increased in the blood of the AM group compared with that of the D0 group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F-H.

claim: The bacterial richness (observed species and ace) of the gut microbiota were decreased at 2 d p.i.
source: The results showed that the bacterial richness (observed species and ace) and the diversity (Simpson index and Shannon index) of the gut microbiota were decreased at 2 d p.i., while they were increased at AM p.i. (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: The diversity (Simpson index and Shannon index) of the gut microbiota were decreased at 2 d p.i.
source: The results showed that the bacterial richness (observed species and ace) and the diversity (Simpson index and Shannon index) of the gut microbiota were decreased at 2 d p.i., while they were increased at AM p.i. (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The bacterial richness and diversity of the gut microbiota were increased at AM p.i.
source: The results showed that the bacterial richness (observed species and ace) and the diversity (Simpson index and Shannon index) of the gut microbiota were decreased at 2 d p.i., while they were increased at AM p.i. (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: The composition of the gut microbiota in the AM group was significantly different from that in the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the composition of the gut microbiota in the AM group was significantly different from that in the D0 group (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: There was a large degree of dispersion among different individuals 2 d p.i.
source: There was a large degree of dispersion among different individuals 2 d p.i. (Figure 2F), and the composition of the gut microbiota in the D2 group was also different from that of the other two groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The composition of the gut microbiota in the D2 group was different from that of the other two groups.
source: There was a large degree of dispersion among different individuals 2 d p.i. (Figure 2F), and the composition of the gut microbiota in the D2 group was also different from that of the other two groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by PCoA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The abundance of Proteobacteria was increased in the AM group.
source: The results showed that the abundance of Proteobacteria was increased in the AM group (Figure 2I and K), while the abundances of Lactobacillus and Allobaculum were decreased compared with those in the D0 group (Figure 2I, L, and M).
evidence: Supported by LEfSe analysis and relative abundance data shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: The abundances of Lactobacillus and Allobaculum were decreased in the AM group compared with those in the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the abundance of Proteobacteria was increased in the AM group (Figure 2I and K), while the abundances of Lactobacillus and Allobaculum were decreased compared with those in the D0 group (Figure 2I, L, and M).
evidence: Supported by LEfSe analysis and relative abundance data shown in Figure 2I, L, and M.

claim: The ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes showed no difference in the D0 and AM groups.
source: Although the relative abundance of Firmicutes seemed to gradually decrease after Leptospira infection (Figure 2H), the ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes showed no difference in the D0 and AM groups (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The intestinal barrier is essential for maintaining intestinal homeostasis.
source: The intestinal barrier is essential for maintaining intestinal homeostasis (Turner, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turner, 2009.

claim: Epithelial tight junctions define the paracellular permeability of the intestinal barrier, which is related to some tight junction proteins, such as claudins, occludin, and zona occludens 1 (Zo-1).
source: Epithelial tight junctions define the paracellular permeability of the intestinal barrier, which is related to some tight junction proteins, such as claudins, occludin, and zona occludens 1 (Zo-1) (Horowitz et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horowitz et al., 2023.

claim: The intestinal permeability of hamsters was increased significantly after Leptospira infection.
source: The results showed that the intestinal permeability of hamsters was increased significantly after infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by FITC-dextran permeability assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The gene expression of Claudin-2 was increased in the AM group compared with the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the gene expression of Claudin-2 was increased, while the gene expression of Claudin-3, JAMA, ZO-1, and Mucin-2 was decreased in the AM group compared with the D0 group (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The gene expression of Claudin-3, JAMA, ZO-1, and Mucin-2 was decreased in the AM group compared with the D0 group.
source: The results showed that the gene expression of Claudin-2 was increased, while the gene expression of Claudin-3, JAMA, ZO-1, and Mucin-2 was decreased in the AM group compared with the D0 group (Figure 3B–F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3B-D and F.

claim: Damaged intestinal structure may increase the translocation of pathobionts.
source: Damaged intestinal structure may increase the translocation of pathobionts (Muñoz et al., 2019; Bertocchi et al., 2021), and our 16S rRNA sequencing showed an increase in Proteobacteria in the AM group.
evidence: Supported by citations to Muñoz et al., 2019 and Bertocchi et al., 2021.

claim: The intestinal epithelium of the AM group had more bacteria than that of the D0 and D2 groups.
source: First, we found that the intestinal epithelium of the AM group had more bacteria than that of the D0 and D2 groups, as determined by the EUB 338 probe, which was supposed to hybridize with all bacteria (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The intestinal epithelium of the AM group had γ-Proteobacteria that was not colocalized with leptospires.
source: The results showed that the intestinal epithelium of the AM group indeed had γ-Proteobacteria that was not colocalized with leptospires (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by FISH and IF data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No bacteria were recovered from the blood by aerobic or anaerobic culture on LB and MacConkey agar plates.
source: However, no bacteria were recovered from the blood by aerobic or anaerobic culture on LB and MacConkey agar plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 16S rRNA sequencing analysis indicated that the richness of the gut microbiota decreased after antibiotic treatment.
source: 16S rRNA sequencing analysis indicated that the richness of the gut microbiota decreased after antibiotic treatment (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The diversity of the gut microbiota in the Abx-treated hamsters was lower than that of the control group.
source: In addition, the diversity of the gut microbiota in the Abx-treated hamsters was lower than that of the control group, and this change in diversity was reversed by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The change in diversity caused by antibiotic treatment was reversed by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT).
source: In addition, the diversity of the gut microbiota in the Abx-treated hamsters was lower than that of the control group, and this change in diversity was reversed by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Antibiotic treatment increased the relative abundance of Proteobacteria.
source: Antibiotic treatment changed the composition of the gut microbiota in hamsters (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), leading to the expansion of Proteobacteria and a decrease in Bacteroidota (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: Antibiotic treatment decreased the relative abundance of Bacteroidota.
source: Antibiotic treatment changed the composition of the gut microbiota in hamsters (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), leading to the expansion of Proteobacteria and a decrease in Bacteroidota (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: Supported by 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The survival time of Abx-treated hamsters was significantly reduced after infection with 106 leptospires.
source: The survival time of Abx-treated hamsters was significantly reduced after infection with 106 leptospires (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The leptospiral load of the Abx group was significantly increased compared with that of the control group.
source: The results showed that the leptospiral load of the Abx group was significantly increased compared with that of the control group, and this increase was partially reversed by FMT (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The increase in leptospiral load caused by antibiotic treatment was partially reversed by FMT.
source: The results showed that the leptospiral load of the Abx group was significantly increased compared with that of the control group, and this increase was partially reversed by FMT (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Abx treatment slightly increased the gene expression of TNF-α and IL-1β compared with those of the untreated group.
source: Abx treatment slightly increased the gene expression of TNF-α and IL-1β compared with those of the untreated group.
evidence: This is an observation from the study, though specific figure reference is not provided in this sentence.

claim: The Abx-treated infection group exhibited higher expression of TNF-α and IL-1β than the untreated infection group.
source: Consistent with this result, the Abx-treated infection group exhibited higher expression of TNF-α and IL-1β than the untreated infection group, which was also partially reversed by FMT (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: The higher expression of TNF-α and IL-1β in the Abx-treated infection group was partially reversed by FMT.
source: Consistent with this result, the Abx-treated infection group exhibited higher expression of TNF-α and IL-1β than the untreated infection group, which was also partially reversed by FMT (Figure 5K and L).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5K and L.

claim: Leptospira infection significantly increased the gene expression of IL-10 compared with that of the untreated group.
source: Although Leptospira infection significantly increased the gene expression of IL-10 compared with that of the untreated group, there was no significant difference among the control infection group, the Abx-treated infection group, and the FMT infection group (Figure 5M).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: There was no significant difference in IL-10 gene expression among the control infection group, the Abx-treated infection group, and the FMT infection group.
source: Although Leptospira infection significantly increased the gene expression of IL-10 compared with that of the untreated group, there was no significant difference among the control infection group, the Abx-treated infection group, and the FMT infection group (Figure 5M).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Gut dysbiosis is a major determinant of endotoxemia via dysfunction of the intestinal barrier scaffold, which is a prerequisite for LPS translocation into systemic circulation.
source: Gut dysbiosis is a major determinant of endotoxemia via dysfunction of the intestinal barrier scaffold, which is a prerequisite for LPS translocation into systemic circulation (Violi et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Violi et al., 2023.

claim: Gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in alcoholic steatohepatitis.
source: A previous study demonstrated that gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in alcoholic steatohepatitis (Szabo, 2015), white adipose tissue inflammation (Caesar et al., 2012), and peripheral inflammation (Lappi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szabo, 2015.

claim: Gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in white adipose tissue inflammation.
source: A previous study demonstrated that gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in alcoholic steatohepatitis (Szabo, 2015), white adipose tissue inflammation (Caesar et al., 2012), and peripheral inflammation (Lappi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caesar et al., 2012.

claim: Gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in peripheral inflammation.
source: A previous study demonstrated that gut-derived LPS was a central mediator in alcoholic steatohepatitis (Szabo, 2015), white adipose tissue inflammation (Caesar et al., 2012), and peripheral inflammation (Lappi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lappi et al., 2013.

claim: Cytokine storms are characteristic of severe leptospirosis.
source: Cytokine storms are characteristic of severe leptospirosis (Cagliero et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cagliero et al., 2018.

claim: The LPS level was higher in the serum of the AM group than that of the D0 group.
source: We found that the LPS level was higher in the serum of the AM group than that of the D0 group (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by LPS measurement data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fecal filtration from uninfected hamsters and AM hamsters both upregulated the gene expression of IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4.
source: The results showed that fecal filtration from uninfected hamsters and AM hamsters both upregulated the gene expression of IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4, while only fecal filtration from AM hamsters upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Only fecal filtration from AM hamsters upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α.
source: The results showed that fecal filtration from uninfected hamsters and AM hamsters both upregulated the gene expression of IL-1β, IL-10, and TLR4, while only fecal filtration from AM hamsters upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The serum of uninfected hamsters significantly increased the transcription of TNF-α.
source: The serum of uninfected hamsters significantly increased the transcription of TNF-α (Figure 6F), while the serum of AM hamsters only slightly upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The serum of AM hamsters only slightly upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α.
source: The serum of uninfected hamsters significantly increased the transcription of TNF-α (Figure 6F), while the serum of AM hamsters only slightly upregulated the gene expression of TNF-α (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Serum from uninfected hamsters and AM hamsters promoted the transcription of IL-1β.
source: Serum from uninfected hamsters and AM hamsters promoted the transcription of IL-1β (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Only the serum of AM hamsters significantly upregulated the gene expression of IL-10 and TLR4.
source: However, only the serum of AM hamsters significantly upregulated the gene expression of IL-10 and TLR4 (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: Cytokine responses to heat-killed leptospires were not inhibited by polymyxin B.
